topics.title: Measuring with hand spans and steps

learn.hook: How long is your desk? Use your hand span and find out!
points: Length tells how long, how tall or how far something is.
We can measure with body parts: hand spans for a desk, footsteps for a room, arm lengths for a cloth.
A hand span is the stretch from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger.
Different people get different answers, because hand spans are not the same size. A child's span is smaller than a teacher's.
To compare lengths, place things side by side: the longest ponytail, a string as long as the window.

example.q: Teacher measures the table as 6 spans. Riya measures it as 9 spans. Who has the bigger hand span?
steps: The same table needs fewer of a bigger unit.

learn.reallife: Tailors used to measure cloth by arm lengths. Now they use a measuring tape so everyone gets the same answer.

games.title: Measuring facts
items: A bigger hand span gives a smaller count.
Everyone's hand span is the same.
Length tells how long or tall something is.
Footsteps are good for measuring a pencil.
A pencil is too short for footsteps.

quiz.q: What does length tell us?
options: How long, tall or far something is
quiz.explain: Length is about how long, tall or far.

quiz.q: Which is best to measure the length of a classroom?
quiz.explain: A room is long, so footsteps are quicker.

quiz.q: Ravi measures a bench as 8 spans. His father measures it as 5 spans. Why are they different?
options: Their hand spans are different sizes
quiz.explain: Father's span is bigger, so fewer spans fit.

quiz.q: A desk is 4 spans long. Two desks side by side are how many spans?
quiz.explain: 4 + 4 = 8 spans.

quiz.q: Meena's ribbon is 7 spans and Gita's is 5 spans (same person measuring). Whose is longer?
quiz.explain: 7 spans is more than 5 spans.

quiz.q: How can you find the longest ponytail in your class without a ruler?
options: Stand the girls side by side and compare
quiz.explain: Comparing side by side shows which is longest.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up height with ponytail length

quiz.q: Raju's room is 12 footsteps long. Mira's room is 9 footsteps (same person). How many more footsteps is Raju's room?
Why do people get different hand-span counts for the same table?
options: Their hands are of different sizes
quiz.explain: This is why we need a common unit everyone agrees on.

teach.ask: Gappu and his mother measured a twig with their wings and got different answers. Why?
teach.praise: Our wings are different sizes, so we need a common unit! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Are our wings the same size?

learn.hook: How far is it from one classroom wall to the other? Steps, a rope, or a stick?
points: To find the distance between two walls, walk heel to toe, or lay a rope or stick again and again, and count.
A good method has no gaps and no overlaps, and uses the same unit every time.
To find the longest and shortest paper strings, place them side by side with one end matching.
To decorate a board, count how many strings fit around its border: top + bottom + 2 sides.

example.q: A board's border is 4 strings on top, 4 on the bottom and 2 on each side. How many strings in all?

learn.reallife: Painters and carpenters measure walls with long tapes before buying paint or wood.

games.title: Lengths
items: Thread to sew on a button
Kite string on a full reel

games.title: Good measuring
items: Leaving gaps between steps gives a correct count.
Gaps make the count too small.
Line up one end of each string to compare.
Then the other ends show which is longest.
Using a stick again and again needs a mark where it ends each time.
Then there is no overlap or gap.

quiz.q: What is the best way to compare paper strings?
options: Line up one end of each and see where the other ends are
quiz.explain: Matching one end shows clearly which is longest.
quiz.mistake: Does not line up the ends

quiz.q: Rohit walks heel to toe across the room: 20 steps. Asha walks with big gaps: 14 steps. Whose count is better?
options: Rohit's, as there are no gaps
quiz.explain: Heel-to-toe has no gaps, so it measures correctly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the smaller count is better

quiz.q: A rope fits 6 times between two walls. Another rope twice as long would fit how many times?
quiz.explain: A longer rope fits fewer times: 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
steps: Twice as long → half as many

quiz.q: A board border needs 5 strings on the top, 5 on the bottom and 3 on each side. How many strings?
Which method gives the SAME answer for everyone measuring a wall?
quiz.explain: Everyone using the same stick gets the same count.
quiz.mistake: Thinks body units are the same for all

quiz.q: Strings: red 7 spans, blue 4 spans, green 9 spans. Which is shortest?
quiz.explain: 4 spans is the smallest.

quiz.q: Same strings (7, 4, 9 spans). How many spans longer is green than blue?
Ram lays a stick 8 times along a wall but the stick overlaps a bit each time. Is the real length more or less than 8 sticks?
quiz.explain: Overlaps mean each stick covers less new wall, so 8 sticks cover less than 8 full lengths. The wall is less than 8 sticks long.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to measure his branch with a twig. What should he be careful about?
teach.praise: No gaps, no overlaps, same twig every time! Chirp!
teach.nudge: What happens if I leave gaps?

learn.hook: Cut a thread exactly as long as this line. Not longer, not shorter!
points: To cut a thread as long as a line, lay it along the line from one end to the other and cut where the line ends.
To draw a string longer than a given one, go past its end. Shorter? Stop before the end.
To complete the other half of a moustache, make it the same length as the first half.
To choose the longest string, compare directly: put them side by side with the ends matching.

example.q: One half of a drawn moustache is 3 boxes long. How long should the other half be?

learn.reallife: Tailors match sleeve lengths so both sleeves of a kurta are equal.

games.title: Match it
items: To match a line, start the thread at one end of the line.
Then cut at the other end.
A longer string goes past the end of the given one.
Both halves of a moustache can be different lengths.
To compare, ends must be lined up.

games.title: Longer or shorter than a 5-box line?

quiz.q: A line is 6 boxes long. Which thread matches it?
quiz.explain: Same length means same number of boxes.

quiz.q: Draw a string longer than a 4-box string. How many boxes could it be?
quiz.explain: 6 is more than 4.

quiz.q: Draw a string shorter than an 8-box string. How many boxes could it be?
quiz.explain: 5 is less than 8.

quiz.q: A moustache's left half is 4 boxes. The right half is 3 boxes. How many boxes must be added to the right?
Three strings are lined up at one end. Red ends at 9, blue at 12, green at 10. Which is longest?
quiz.explain: 12 goes furthest.

quiz.q: A full moustache has two equal halves of 5 boxes each. How many boxes long is it in all?
Mohan starts his thread a little after the start of the line and cuts at the end of the line. His thread is…
quiz.explain: He started late, so his thread misses a bit at the start.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the late start

quiz.q: Raju's string is 3 boxes longer than a 6-box string. How many boxes long is Raju's string?

teach.ask: Gappu needs a worm exactly as long as his twig. How should he check?
teach.praise: Put them side by side, ends together. If they end at the same place, they match! Chirp!

learn.hook: Will the big table fit through the door? We cannot lift it to try. Use a string!
points: When two things cannot be placed side by side, use a third thing, like a string or stick.
Measure the table's width with a string and mark it. Then hold the same string against the door.
If the door is wider than the string mark, the table will fit.
Build a block bridge, measure the gap under it, and guess which toys will pass under.
A tall truck or a long ladder held upright may not pass through a school gate.

example.q: A string matches the width of a cupboard. When held across a door, the string is longer than the door is wide. Will the cupboard pass?
steps: The cupboard is as wide as the string.
The door is narrower than the string.

learn.reallife: Before buying a sofa or a fridge, families measure the door to check that it will fit through!

games.title: Indirect comparison
items: A string can carry a length from one place to another.
We must always lift things to compare them.
A string or stick can help.
If the string is shorter than the gap, the object can pass.
A bridge 4 blocks high lets a 6-block toy pass under it.

quiz.q: How can you compare the width of a table and a door without moving the table?
options: Use a string to measure one and compare with the other
quiz.explain: The string carries the length across.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you must move the table

quiz.q: The string for the table is shorter than the door's width. What does this tell us?
quiz.explain: The door is wider than the table.

quiz.q: A bridge has a gap 5 blocks high. A toy is 3 blocks tall. Can it pass?
quiz.explain: 3 is less than 5, so it fits under.

quiz.q: A gap under the bridge is 4 blocks high. Which toy CANNOT pass?
quiz.explain: 6 is more than 4.

quiz.q: A pole is 7 sticks tall and the gate is 5 sticks tall. How many sticks too tall is the pole to pass standing up?
Which might NOT pass through a school gate?
quiz.explain: A truck is too tall and wide for most school gates.

quiz.q: Raju's string matches his window's width. It is longer than Mira's window. Whose window is wider?
quiz.explain: Raju's window is as wide as the string, and the string is longer than Mira's window.

quiz.q: Why do we need a third object like a string?
options: When two things cannot be put side by side
quiz.explain: It lets us compare lengths in different places.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know if his nest will fit in a hole in the tree. He cannot carry the nest. What can he do?
teach.praise: Measure the nest with a grass blade, then hold it at the hole! Chirp!
teach.nudge: What can I carry to the hole instead of the nest?

learn.hook: Is your arm span the same as your height? Let us test it like scientists!
points: Some body measures are often close to each other. We test them to see if they are true for everyone.
Test 1: wrap a string around your head. Is it about 3 of your hand spans?
Test 2: is your forearm (elbow to wrist) about as long as your foot?
Test 3: stretch your arms wide. Is your arm span about the same as your height?
Test many people and record 'yes' or 'no'. If even one person does not fit, it is not true for ALL.

example.q: 8 friends test arm span = height. 7 say yes and 1 says no. Is it true for all?
example.answer: No, it is true for most but not all

learn.reallife: Artists drawing people use body measures like these to get the shape right.

games.title: Testing ideas
items: To test an idea, we try it on many people.
If one person does not fit, it is not true for all.
We can test arm span with a string.
Measure the span and then compare with height.
Testing only yourself proves it for everyone.

quiz.q: How can you test if your arm span equals your height?
options: Measure both with a string and compare
quiz.explain: A string shows both lengths so you can compare them.

quiz.q: How can you check if your head is about 3 hand spans around?
options: Wrap a string around your head and measure it in spans
quiz.explain: The string gives the distance around, and then we measure it with spans.

quiz.q: Forearm means…
quiz.explain: The forearm is the part from the elbow to the wrist.

quiz.q: 15 children test 'forearm = foot'. 12 say yes. How many say no?
In the test above, is 'forearm = foot' true for ALL 15 children?
quiz.explain: All means every one. 3 did not fit.

quiz.q: Riya's head is 3 spans around. Her brother's head is also 3 of HIS spans. Are their heads the same size?
options: Not necessarily: their spans may be different
quiz.explain: 3 spans each, but spans are different sizes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks spans are the same for all

quiz.q: Which is the best way to test an idea about body measures?
options: Try it on many people and record
quiz.explain: Many people give a fairer answer.

quiz.q: 6 friends tested arm span = height. All 6 said yes. Can we be sure it is true for every person in the world?
quiz.explain: It is true for these 6, but other people may be different.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a small test proves it for all

teach.ask: Gappu says 'My wings are as long as my body, so it is true for all birds!' What would you tell him?
teach.praise: I should test many birds before I say ALL! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Is one bird enough to be sure?

learn.hook: Hand spans gave everyone a different answer. The metre gives everyone the SAME answer!
points: We need a standard unit so that everyone gets the same measure.
The metre (m) is a standard unit of length. A metre rod or a measuring tape shows 1 metre.
Make a one-metre rope: lay a rope along a metre rod and cut it at the end.
Mark 1 metre from the floor on a wall. Stand against it to see if you are taller or shorter than 1 metre.
A door is about 2 metres tall. A classroom may be about 6 to 8 metres long.

example.q: A rope is laid along a metre rod 3 times to measure a mat. How long is the mat?

learn.reallife: Cloth shops sell cloth by the metre, and sports tracks are measured in metres.

games.title: Metre facts
items: A metre is a standard unit of length.
It is the same for everyone.
A hand span is a standard unit.
Hand spans differ from person to person.
A measuring tape can show 1 metre.

items.q: Mat 2 m, 3 mats in a row

quiz.q: Why do we need a standard unit like the metre?
options: So everyone gets the same measure
quiz.explain: Body units differ, but a metre is the same for all.

quiz.q: Which tool shows 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A metre rod is exactly 1 metre long.
quiz.mistake: Picks a tool for weight or time

quiz.q: How do you make a 1-metre rope?
options: Lay it along a metre rod and cut at the end
quiz.explain: Matching it to the metre rod makes it exactly 1 metre.

quiz.q: A mat is 2 m long. Three mats in a row are how long?
Ravi stands against a 1-metre mark on the wall. His head is above the mark. What does this tell us?
quiz.explain: Above the mark means taller.

quiz.q: A rope is 5 m long. 2 m is cut off. How much is left?
Which is about 1 metre long?
options: A big stride of a grown-up
quiz.explain: A big stride is about 1 metre.
quiz.mistake: Picks something too short or too long

quiz.q: Tina measures her room with a metre tape: 4 m. Her friend measures it with the same tape. What will the friend get?
quiz.explain: A standard unit gives the same answer for everyone.
quiz.mistake: Thinks results differ like hand spans

teach.ask: Gappu asks why we use metres and not wing lengths. What would you tell him?
teach.praise: A metre is the same for everyone, but wings are different! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Is a wing length the same for every bird?

learn.hook: Is your friend taller than a metre rod? Is a door? Is a pencil? Let us sort!
points: Stand friends next to a 1-metre mark. Sort them: taller than 1 m, or shorter than 1 m.
Many Class 3 children are a little taller than 1 metre.
Objects can be longer than, shorter than or about equal to 1 metre.
Longer than 1 m: a door, a bed, a classroom. Shorter: a pencil, a book, a shoe. About 1 m: a metre rod, a big stride.

steps: A bed is long: longer than 1 m.
A metre rod is exactly 1 m.
example.answer: Longer: bed; shorter: eraser; equal: metre rod

learn.reallife: At amusement parks, some rides have a height mark. You must be taller than it to ride!

items.q: Taller 9, shorter 6. How many more taller?

quiz.q: Which is longer than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A door is about 2 metres tall.

quiz.q: Which is shorter than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A notebook is much shorter than a metre.

quiz.q: Which is about 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A metre rod is exactly 1 metre.

quiz.q: In a class, 18 children are taller than 1 m and 7 are shorter. How many children?
Same class: how many more are taller than 1 m than shorter?
Ajay's head is below the 1-metre mark. He is…
quiz.explain: Below the mark means shorter.

quiz.q: A bed is about 2 m long. Is that more or less than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: 2 metres is more than 1 metre.

quiz.q: Which list has ONLY things longer than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A bus, a door and a bed are all longer than 1 m.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to sort his friends by height using 1 metre. How should he do it?
teach.praise: Make a 1-metre mark, then sort: above it is taller, below is shorter! Chirp!
teach.nudge: What should I compare each friend with?

learn.hook: Fold a 1-metre rope in half. Now you have a half-metre! Fold again for a quarter-metre!
points: Fold a 1-metre rope in half and cut: each piece is half a metre.
Fold the half-metre in half again: each piece is a quarter metre.
2 half metres make 1 metre. 4 quarter metres make 1 metre. 2 quarter metres make a half metre.
Sort objects: less than a quarter metre (an eraser), about half a metre (a school bag), about 1 metre.
Measure a long jump with a metre rope: 1 metre and a half metre is one and a half metres.

example.q: Leela jumps 1 metre rope + 1 half-metre rope + 1 quarter-metre rope. How far?
steps: 1 m + half m = one and a half m

learn.reallife: Cloth shops sell half a metre or a quarter metre of ribbon too.

quiz.q: How do you make a half-metre rope from a 1-metre rope?
options: Fold it in half and cut
quiz.explain: Folding in half gives two equal halves.

quiz.q: How many half metres make 1 metre?
quiz.explain: 2 halves make a whole.

quiz.q: How many quarter metres make 1 metre?
quiz.explain: 4 quarters make a whole.

quiz.q: How many quarter metres make a half metre?
quiz.explain: 2 quarters = 1 half.

quiz.q: Which is about half a metre long?
quiz.explain: A school bag is about half a metre tall.

quiz.q: Which is LESS than a quarter metre?
quiz.explain: An eraser is very small.

quiz.q: A throw is measured with 3 metre ropes and 1 half-metre rope. How far?
quiz.explain: 3 m + half m = 3 and a half m.
quiz.mistake: Counts the half rope as a full metre

quiz.q: A ribbon is 4 quarter metres long. How long is it?
quiz.explain: 4 quarters make 1 whole metre.

teach.ask: Gappu has a 1-metre vine. How can he get a quarter-metre piece?
teach.praise: Fold in half, then fold in half again: a quarter metre! Chirp!
teach.nudge: How many folds do I need?

learn.hook: Close your eyes and cut a thread you think is 1 metre long. Now check with a metre rod. How close were you?
points: Estimate 1 metre by cutting a thread, then check it with a metre rod.
To cut a rope into 4 equal pieces, you need only 3 cuts.
In general, the number of cuts is one less than the number of pieces.
Count how many of your footsteps make 1 metre. It may be 4 or 5 for a child.
Measure a classroom wall with a metre rope: lay it end to end and count.

example.q: How many cuts are needed to cut a ribbon into 6 equal pieces?

learn.reallife: A carpenter cutting a plank into pieces must plan the number of cuts, not just the pieces.

games.title: Metre fun facts
items: Checking an estimate with a metre rod shows how close we were.
Everyone takes the same number of footsteps for 1 metre.
Laying a metre rope 5 times along a wall means the wall is about 5 m.

quiz.q: How many cuts make 4 equal pieces of a rope?
quiz.explain: Pieces − 1 = cuts. 4 − 1 = 3.

quiz.q: How many pieces do 2 cuts make?
quiz.explain: Cuts + 1 = pieces.

quiz.q: Sita's guessed thread is a bit longer than the metre rod. What was her estimate?
quiz.explain: Longer than the rod means more than 1 m.

quiz.q: Kabir takes 5 footsteps to cover 1 metre. How many footsteps for 3 metres?
A metre rope is laid along a wall 8 times. How long is the wall?
quiz.explain: Each lay is 1 metre: 8 × 1 = 8 m.

quiz.q: Why might Ria and her teacher take different numbers of steps to make 1 metre?
quiz.explain: Bigger steps mean fewer steps.

quiz.q: A ribbon is cut into 10 equal pieces. How many cuts?
Raju's estimate of 1 metre was exactly as long as the metre rod. What does this mean?
quiz.explain: Same length as the rod means exactly 1 metre.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to cut a worm-shaped noodle into 5 equal pieces. How many cuts must he make?
teach.praise: 4 cuts give 5 pieces: one less cut than pieces! Chirp!
teach.nudge: For 2 pieces, how many cuts do I need?

learn.hook: 2, 4, 6, 8... who do we appreciate? Number patterns, of course!
points: A pattern follows a rule again and again.
Some patterns grow by adding: 2, 4, 6, 8 (add 2 each time).
Some patterns get smaller by taking away: 50, 45, 40 (take away 5 each time).
Find the rule by looking at how each number changes to the next.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. They take turns: even, odd, even, odd.
learn.reallife: House numbers on one side of a street often go 2, 4, 6, 8 and on the other side 1, 3, 5, 7.

quiz.q: What comes next? 5, 10, 15, 20, ___
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 5'. 20 + 5 = 25.

quiz.q: What is the rule? 30, 27, 24, 21
quiz.explain: Each number is 3 less than the one before: 30 − 3 = 27, 27 − 3 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Sees a jump of 3 but misses that the numbers are getting smaller

quiz.q: Find the missing number: 6, 12, ___, 24, 30
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 6'. 12 + 6 = 18, and 18 + 6 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Uses a jump of 2 or 4 instead of 6

quiz.q: What comes next? 1, 4, 7, 10, ___
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 3'. 10 + 3 = 13.

quiz.q: Which number is EVEN?
quiz.explain: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. 58 ends in 8.
quiz.mistake: Looks at the tens digit instead of the ones digit

quiz.q: At the party, Riya puts 2 balloons on the first chair, 4 on the second and 6 on the third. How many on the fourth chair?
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 2'. 6 + 2 = 8.

quiz.q: What comes next? 50, 40, 30, ___
quiz.explain: The rule is 'take away 10'. 30 − 10 = 20.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pattern goes up instead of down

quiz.q: Arjun's pattern is 2, 4, 8, 16, ___. Each number is double the one before. What comes next?
quiz.explain: Double 16 is 16 + 16 = 32.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 each time instead of doubling

teach.ask: Gappu sees 4, 8, 12, 16 on the party board. How can he find the next number?
teach.praise: Add 4 each time! The next number is 20!
teach.nudge: How does each number change to the next one?

learn.hook: Party flags, bangles and rangoli all have patterns. Can you guess what comes next?
points: A repeating pattern has a part that comes again and again: 🔴🔵🔴🔵.
The part that repeats is called the core. In red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, the core is red, blue, blue.
A growing pattern gets bigger at each step: 1 dot, 2 dots, 3 dots.
To find what comes next, find the core or the rule first.

example.q: Party flags go: green, yellow, yellow, green, yellow, yellow, ___. What comes next?
steps: The core is green, yellow, yellow.
After the second yellow, the core starts again.

learn.reallife: Borders of saris, bead necklaces and paper chains for parties all show patterns.

items.text: A, B, B, A, B, B, ___

games.title: Pattern detective
items: Red, blue, red, blue is a repeating pattern.
Red, blue comes again and again.
A growing pattern gets bigger at each step.
In red, white, red, white ..., the 6th bead is white.
Red is in places 1, 3, 5. White is in places 2, 4, 6.
Circle, square, circle, square ...: the 5th shape is a square.

quiz.q: What comes next? 🔴🟢🔴🟢🔴___
quiz.explain: The core is 🔴🟢. After 🔴 comes 🟢.
quiz.mistake: Repeats the last colour instead of following the core

quiz.q: Bangles go: red, red, gold, red, red, gold. What is the core of this pattern?
quiz.explain: The part that repeats is red, red, gold.
quiz.mistake: Misses one of the reds in the core

quiz.q: Rangoli dots go: 1 dot, 3 dots, 5 dots, 7 dots. How many dots come next?
quiz.explain: Each step adds 2 dots. 7 + 2 = 9.

quiz.q: A paper chain goes pink, blue, pink, blue ... What colour is the 8th ring?
quiz.explain: Pink is in places 1, 3, 5, 7. Blue is in places 2, 4, 6, 8. So the 8th ring is blue.

quiz.q: Which of these is a GROWING pattern?
quiz.explain: In ⭐, ⭐⭐, ⭐⭐⭐ each step has one more star, so it grows.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up repeating patterns with growing patterns

quiz.q: Kabir sets plates: big, small, small, big, small, small, big, ___. What comes next?
quiz.explain: The core is big, small, small. After 'big' comes 'small'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pattern just takes turns, big then small then big

quiz.q: Tiles: step 1 has 2 tiles, step 2 has 4 tiles, step 3 has 6 tiles. How many tiles in step 4?
quiz.explain: Each step adds 2 tiles. 6 + 2 = 8.

quiz.q: A border goes triangle, circle, square, triangle, circle, square ... Which shape is 7th?
quiz.explain: The core has 3 shapes. Places 1, 4 and 7 are triangles.

teach.ask: Gappu made a necklace: red bead, yellow bead, yellow bead, red bead, yellow bead... What bead comes next and how do you know?
teach.praise: Red, yellow, yellow keeps repeating, so yellow comes next! My necklace looks lovely.
teach.nudge: Which part of my necklace keeps coming again?

learn.hook: Fold a paper butterfly down the middle. Both wings match perfectly. That's symmetry!
points: A shape is symmetrical if one half is a mirror image of the other half.
The fold line that makes two matching halves is called the line of symmetry.
Letters like A, H, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y have matching halves when folded along a standing line down the middle.
Some shapes have more than one line of symmetry. A square has 4. A circle has many.
Rangoli and kolam designs are often symmetrical.

example.q: How many lines of symmetry does a long rectangle, like a door, have?
steps: Fold it along a standing line down the middle: the halves match.
Fold it along a sleeping line across the middle: the halves match.
Fold it corner to corner: the halves do NOT match.

learn.reallife: Butterflies, leaves, diyas, the Taj Mahal and many rangoli designs are symmetrical.

games.title: Mirror, mirror
items: A square has 4 lines of symmetry.
2 folds through the middle of the sides and 2 folds corner to corner.
No fold makes the two halves of F match.
A circle has many lines of symmetry.
Any fold through the centre makes two matching halves.
A long rectangle, like a door, has 4 lines of symmetry.
It has only 2. Corner-to-corner folds do not match.
The two halves of a symmetrical shape match exactly.

quiz.q: What do we call the fold line that splits a shape into two matching halves?
quiz.explain: A line of symmetry divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the line of symmetry with the edge of the shape

quiz.q: Which letter is symmetrical?
quiz.explain: Fold H down the middle and both halves match. F, G and R do not have matching halves.
quiz.mistake: Picks a letter without trying to fold it in the mind

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
quiz.explain: A square can be folded top to bottom, side to side and along both corner-to-corner lines. That makes 4.

quiz.q: Riya folds a paper heart down the middle and the two halves match. The heart is ___.
quiz.explain: When two halves match exactly after folding, the shape is symmetrical.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect matching halves with symmetry

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT symmetrical?
quiz.explain: J has a hook on one side only, so no fold makes its halves match.
quiz.mistake: Misses the word NOT in the question

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a long rectangle, like a door, have?
quiz.explain: Folding down the middle and across the middle both work. Corner-to-corner folds do not.
steps: Corner to corner: does not match
quiz.mistake: Thinks a rectangle has 4 lines like a square

quiz.q: Aisha drew half of a rangoli flower. To make it symmetrical, the other half must be ___.
options: a mirror copy of the first half
quiz.explain: In a symmetrical design, one half is a mirror image of the other.
quiz.mistake: Thinks symmetry means just filling the space

quiz.q: Which word is made ONLY of letters that match when folded down the middle?
quiz.explain: T, O, M and A all match when folded down the middle. MANGO has N and G, CAKE has C, K and E, PIZZA has P and Z. These do not.
quiz.mistake: Checks only some of the letters

teach.ask: Gappu found a butterfly and a leaf. His friend says they are symmetrical. What does that mean?
teach.praise: Fold it in the middle and both halves match! Butterflies are symmetrical!
teach.nudge: What happens to the two halves when I fold it down the middle?
